article.title: Jev Engineering: The Model That Refuses to Talk, and Why That's the Whole Point

blocks.text: A company spent two years saying nothing, then launched a model that still says nothing, on purpose, and within three days strangers had it finding flights for less than half a cent and sorting five hundred emails for the price of a stick of gum.

The company is TypeSafe AI. The model is Jev, launched September 15, 2026. It cannot write an email, summarize a document, or generate a line of code. Ask it to write anything, and it simply won't. That's not a gap someone forgot to close. It's the entire product.
The founder who kept asking the wrong question, then found the right one

Jev's creator, Diogo Almeida, co-invented RLHF, the technique that turned raw language models into something like ChatGPT, during his time at OpenAI. He left with two colleagues, Erik Gafni and Sasha Sheng, asking a question that should bother anyone paying attention: if chat models are this good, why hasn't superhuman conversation gotten anyone closer to AGI?

His answer, now backed by a $40M seed round led by DCVC, is that the industry has been renting a Ferrari to sit in traffic. Most of what software needs isn't language. It's judgment. Is this ticket urgent? Which of five workers handles this? Did the test pass? Is this shell command dangerous? None of that needs a paragraph. It needs a fast, calibrated yes.
Every one of those questions has been getting routed through a full language model anyway, because that was the only tool anyone had. Jev is built for the other half of the job.
Before touching any code, there's a three-question test that tells you whether a given decision even belongs to that other half:
Can you write down every valid answer in advance? If the list of acceptable outputs is open-ended, this isn't a Jev decision, it's a writing task.
Would a fast human glance settle it? If judging the situation correctly requires actually thinking, not just recognizing, a classifier isn't the right tool, no matter how cheap it is.
Does this happen often enough for milliseconds and fractions of a cent to matter? A decision you make five times a week doesn't need a 200x speedup. A decision made five thousand times a day does.
Three yeses, and the decision is a real candidate. One no, and the honest move is leaving it exactly where it is.

Run it once, right now, on something real. "Is this support ticket urgent." Every valid answer fits in two words, yes or no. A person glances at the ticket for three seconds and knows. It happens hundreds of times a day. Three yeses. That decision has been costing you a full generation call for something that never needed one.
What actually happens when you send it a question

You give Jev two things: state, and typed questions. State is just the situation, a JSON blob, a log, a transcript, whatever text describes what's happening right now. The questions come in exactly three shapes.

Choice picks one option out of a list you define, up to 255 of them, and returns a probability for every single one. Score places the input on an ordered scale you define and returns a probability-weighted position, which can land between two levels rather than snapping to one. Noul, TypeSafe's own name for a yes/no primitive, returns a number between 0 and 1 representing how true the answer is.

That's the entire vocabulary. No prose to parse. No JSON repair when the model decides to explain itself first. You ask "which team should own this ticket," define engineering, billing, and sales as the only three valid answers, and you get back a probability for each one, in one round trip, evaluated in parallel rather than one token at a time.

The response time TypeSafe reports: 70 to 500 milliseconds. The price: $0.042 per million input tokens, with output tokens free. Compare that to a chat model reasoning through the same classification out loud first, which the company's own benchmarks put at 3 to 329 seconds for the equivalent task.

Three questions, one API call, one round trip. All three get evaluated in parallel against the same state, which is why adding a fourth or fifth question barely moves the latency. Your code decides what happens with the answer:
That last block is the entire architecture in miniature. Jev answers the fuzzy question. Ordinary code, the kind you can unit test, owns every branch after that.
The numbers that made this land, within 72 hours
Marketing claims are cheap. What actually made people pay attention was developers testing it in public within three days of launch, and posting the receipts.

Browser Use wired Jev into an agent that reads a live webpage, decides the next click, and executes it. It found flight results in 7 seconds for $0.0039. Not simulated. A public video, timestamped, at real speed.
A developer named Hassan fed Jev 1,018 real AI research papers and asked it to classify each one into a topic. Total cost: $0.08. Median time per paper: 256 milliseconds.
Riley Brown ran 500 real emails through it for triage, deciding reply, research, wait, or review for each one. Total cost: 3.5 cents.

A developer named Jarrod Watts went further and built a live market-making trading bot on the Monad blockchain, having Jev decide buy or sell against a real on-chain order book every 300-millisecond block. The repository hit 1,000+ GitHub stars in three days, with a public dashboard streaming decisions landing in 81 milliseconds each.

Separately, someone ran Jev as a plugin inside Claude, using it to review which tool calls in a session were actually necessary. It compacted a Claude session from nearly 1 million tokens down to 86,000, in one second. Not a summarization pass. A relevance filter running at Jev speed.
The honest part almost nobody selling this mentions

TypeSafe's own published range is 20 to 200x faster and 40 to 400x cheaper, and one deeper technical breakdown of the stack makes an important correction: those numbers are a ceiling, not a typical result, and treating them as a target instead of a description is how people end up building the wrong architecture.

The real multiplier doesn't come from Jev being 200x faster than an LLM on one call versus one call. It comes from decision density. Picture an agent working through a support ticket end to end: reading the complaint, checking whether it matches a known bug, deciding which team owns it, scoring how urgent it is, and confirming the fix actually resolved things before closing the ticket. Four of those five steps have a bounded, short answer. Only one of them, reading the complaint itself, genuinely needs language. In a standard setup, all five get routed through the same generative model anyway, each one writing out a paragraph of reasoning before landing on an answer that only ever had two or three valid shapes. Pull the four bounded steps out and route them to Jev instead, and you're not making one call faster. You're removing four full-cost generation calls from every single ticket, at volume, all day.
Most agent bills aren't expensive because the work is hard. They're expensive because four out of five steps were never asked to be cheap.

A workflow that's mostly generation, writing a long document from scratch, gets nowhere near the advertised ceiling. A workflow dense with bounded decisions gets close to it. The actual skill is auditing your own agent first to find which decisions were never decisions the language model needed to make.

Here's what that split actually looks like once it's wired in. Every bounded decision gets an acceptance threshold, and anything that doesn't clear it falls back to the model that can actually reason through ambiguity:

A high number back from Jev tells you it's sure. It doesn't tell you it's right, and that gap between certainty and correctness is the entire reason the threshold exists in the first place, set separately for every kind of decision rather than one number reused everywhere.
What it genuinely cannot do, stated as plainly as the claims

Jev cannot break its own answer schema. If you define three valid categories, it will never invent a fourth. TypeSafe describes this as an inability to hallucinate, and that's true, but only under a narrow definition worth being precise about.

It can absolutely choose the wrong valid option, confidently, and there's no error message for that, because returning a confident answer is exactly what it's built to do. Picture a schema built to sort support tickets into "needs a refund," "needs an apology," and "needs escalation," three categories that sound distinct but overlap constantly in practice, since most refund requests also want an apology and plenty of escalations start as simple refund asks. A model forced to pick exactly one from three options that were never truly separate will pick one anyway, every time, with a confidence score that looks identical whether the pick was obvious or a coin flip. The fix isn't a better model. It's rewriting the three categories so they don't secretly describe the same ticket from three different angles.

TypeSafe is fairly direct about where the line sits, once you look past the headline numbers. Jev doesn't generate text or design a strategy from nothing. It can't chain one judgment into the next inside a single call, because every question in a request gets answered in isolation, so a decision that depends on a different decision still needs two separate round trips. It has no business competing at microsecond latency, the kind colocated trading infrastructure runs at.

And none of its speed changes whether an answer was actually correct. Picture a support system where "urgent" and "not urgent" looked like a clean two-way split on paper. Jev sorts a genuine emergency into the wrong queue in 90 milliseconds, confidently, because the wording happened to resemble a hundred false alarms it had correctly ignored before. The mistake didn't get smaller because it arrived fast. It just got expensive faster, and nobody found out until someone went looking for why the ticket sat untouched.
Where this is already shipping in production, right now
LangChain built middleware that runs every proposed tool call through Jev before it executes, blocking risky actions and approving safe ones before the tool call runs:

One line of middleware. Every dangerous tool call now passes through a classifier first, at a fraction of a cent, instead of trusting the same model that wrote the command to also judge whether the command is safe.

Coding tools like Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor have quietly shipped some version of this classifier gate for a while now, buried in the closed-source parts of their own harness. What changed on September 15 is that the same pattern is no longer locked away.
The actual shift underneath the launch

Jev isn't a smarter chat model, and it never tried to be one. It's a bet that most of what software calls intelligence was classification wearing a paragraph as a disguise, billed at generation prices for an answer that only ever had two or three valid shapes.

Before you build anything, open the last agent session you actually ran and count. Every place it paused to decide something, not write something, run it through the three questions from earlier. Most sessions have more of those moments hiding in them than anyone notices on the first pass, right up until they go looking specifically for the pause.

```python
def handle_ticket_routing(ticket_state):
    result = jev.system_one(state=ticket_state, questions=ROUTING_SCHEMA)
    owner_answer = result.answers["owner"]

    if owner_answer.confidence < 0.75:
        return escalate_to_full_model(ticket_state)  # too close to call, ask something that can think

    return owner_answer.choice
```

```python
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain_typesafe.experimental.middleware import AutoModeMiddleware

# Jev checks every tool call before execution.
# Blocks risky actions, approves safe ones. Zero generation tokens spent on the check.
guardrail = AutoModeMiddleware(tools=["bash"])
agent = create_agent("openai:gpt-5.6-luna", middleware=[guardrail])
```
